Can a Portable Power Station Run a Space Heater? (The Honest Math)
AR

Alejandro Rodríguez, MD
Physician (MD, Colombia)

Sep 23, 2026
Sep 25, 2026

Specs verified, runtimes calculated. We don’t lab-test power stations (yet). How we research

Quick answer:
yes, a portable power station can run a space heater if its AC output is higher than the heater’s wattage, but not for long. A typical 1,500 W heater empties a 1,000 Wh power station in about 35 minutes. Even a 3,000 Wh unit lasts under 2 hours. For staying warm during a winter outage, an electric blanket uses a small fraction of the energy and keeps you warm all night.

Runtimes below are calculated estimates assuming 85% of rated capacity is usable and about 10 W of inverter overhead. See How We Research.

The bottom line
Space heater runtime chart
Power station capacity	Heater on low (750 W)	Heater on high (1,500 W)
500 Wh	~34 minutes	~17 minutes (if the inverter can handle it)
1,000 Wh	~67 minutes	~34 minutes
2,000 Wh	~2.2 hours	~68 minutes
3,000 Wh	~3.4 hours	~1.7 hours
Formula: runtime (hours) = (power station Wh × 0.85) ÷ (heater watts + 10 W for the inverter). Heaters with a thermostat cycle off once the room warms up, so real runtime can be somewhat longer in a small, well-insulated room.

There’s also an output requirement: the power station’s continuous AC output must exceed the heater’s wattage. A 1,500 W heater needs a unit rated well above 1,500 W, which rules out most small and mid-size models.

Why heaters drain batteries so fast

Turning electricity into heat takes a lot of power. A 1,500 W space heater uses as much energy in one hour as an average refrigerator uses in a whole day. That’s why the same power station that keeps your fridge cold for 12 hours only runs a heater for about half an hour. For comparison, see our refrigerator runtime guide.

Cooling is the summer version of the same problem, though a small window AC is gentler than a heater: see can a portable power station run a window AC.

Better ways to stay warm on battery power

The trick is to heat people, not rooms.

Option	Typical power	Runtime on 1,000 Wh (estimate)
Electric blanket or heated mattress pad	about 50–100 W	roughly 8–14 hours
Heated throw on the couch	about 50–100 W	roughly 8–14 hours
Small space heater on low	about 750 W	about 67 minutes
Space heater on high	about 1,500 W	about 34 minutes
Check the label on your blanket or pad: many use much less than their maximum once they reach temperature.
Pick one room. Gather everyone in the smallest room with the fewest windows and close the door.
Layer up. Hats, socks and several thin layers hold heat better than one thick one.
Block drafts. Towels along door gaps and blankets over windows help a lot.
Use the heater in short bursts. If you must, warm a small room for 10–15 minutes before bed, then switch to an electric blanket.
Space heater safety rules

Space heaters are a leading cause of home heating fires. If you run one from a power station, the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission’s rules still apply:

Keep anything that can burn, such as curtains, bedding, sofas and clothes, at least 3 feet from the heater.
Plug it directly into the power station’s AC outlet. Never use an extension cord or power strip.
Never leave it running unattended or while you sleep.
Place it on a flat, stable surface where it can’t be knocked over, and choose a model with tip-over and overheat shutoff.

Never heat your home with a gas oven, camp stove, charcoal grill or generator. They produce carbon monoxide, which can kill without warning. See our generator safety guide.

A note from a physician: cold is most dangerous for older adults, infants and people with heart or lung conditions. If your home becomes too cold to stay in safely, go to a warming center or a friend’s home with power rather than trying to heat the house on battery.

Heating with gas? A gas furnace still needs electricity for its blower and controls. See can a portable power station run a gas furnace for runtimes by battery size and how to connect it safely.

Need to stay warm on battery? An electric blanket uses about 60–110 W, a fraction of a space heater. See can a power station run an electric blanket for runtimes by battery size.

Frequently asked questions
What size power station do I need to run a space heater?

For a 1,500 W heater, you need at least about 1,800 W of continuous AC output, and even a 3,000 Wh battery gives you less than 2 hours on high. Use our sizing guide to plan the rest of your needs.

Can solar panels keep a space heater running?
Is an electric blanket safe to run from a power station?
The bottom line

A power station can run a space heater, but only for minutes, not hours. Save your battery for an electric blanket, your refrigerator and your phone, and use a heater only in short, supervised bursts.

U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission, Keep Warm and Safe This Winter.

 What size power station do I need for a space heater?

Can a Portable Power Station Run a Space Heater? | PowerStationMatch 
 Can a Portable Power Station Run a Space Heater ?
 Wattage data verified from manufacturer specs and appliance databases. Last reviewed November 2026 . 
 Technically yes, but it's impractical as a primary heat source. A space heater on high draws ~1,500W continuously with little startup surge, so you need a station with an 1,800W+ inverter. The catch is runtime: at 1,500W, even a 2,000Wh station lasts only about an hour, and a 1,000Wh unit 30-40 minutes. Use it for short, targeted warmth during an outage — and never leave a space heater running unattended.
 How Much Power Does a Space Heater Use?
 Metric Range

 Startup surge 750 – 1600 W 
 DC power possible? No 
 Most electric space heaters run at 750W (low) or 1,500W (high) with little startup surge, since resistive heating elements have no motor. The challenge isn't starting one — it's runtime: resistive heat converts a lot of energy fast, so even a large battery drains in about an hour on high.

 FAQ
 Can a portable power station run a space heater?
 Yes, if the station has an 1,800W+ inverter to handle a 1,500W heater on high (a 750W low setting needs less). There's almost no startup surge because the heating element has no motor. The real limit is runtime — resistive heating is energy-hungry, so a power station can provide short bursts of warmth, not continuous heat for hours.
 How long will a power station run a 1500W space heater?
 About an hour on a 2,000Wh station, and roughly 30-40 minutes on a 1,000Wh unit, at the 1,500W high setting. Running the heater on a 750W low setting roughly doubles those times. Resistive heat drains batteries fast, so plan for short, targeted use.
 What size power station do I need for a space heater?
 For a 1,500W heater, an 1,800W+ continuous inverter; for a 750W heater, around 1,000W+. Surge isn't the issue (heaters have almost none) — capacity is. For any meaningful runtime, choose 2,000Wh or more, or run the heater on low. During an outage, insulation and layering plus a small heater on low is far more practical than trying to heat a room on battery.
 Is it safe to run a space heater on a power station?
 The station itself handles it if its inverter is rated above the heater's wattage. Follow normal heater safety regardless: never leave it unattended, keep it well clear of flammables, and plug it directly into the station rather than through a flimsy extension cord. Because resistive heat drains a battery quickly, treat it as short-term backup warmth, not a furnace replacement.

Can a Power Station Run a Space Heater? (Why It's Usually a Bad Idea) | Lights On Lab Skip to content 
 Can a Power Station Run a Space Heater? (Why It's Usually a Bad Idea)
 D By Daniel Updated November 1, 2026 3 min read 
 Short answer Technically yes, but not for long: a 1,500 W heater empties a 1,000 Wh power station in about 35 minutes. An electric blanket at 50–100 W can last all night instead.
 ⏱️ Get your exact number

 This guide has affiliate links. If you buy through one we may earn a commission, at no cost to you. How this works .
 It’s a common plan: if the power goes out in winter, plug a space heater into the power station. Unfortunately, the numbers don’t work out.
 The math
 A standard space heater uses 1,500 W on high and about 750 W on low. Most power stations with 1,800 W or more of output can technically run one. The problem is how fast the battery empties:

 Runtime = Wh × 0.85 ÷ watts. Heating is about the most energy-hungry thing you can do with electricity. An electric heater turns every watt-hour into heat, but it needs an awful lot of them.
 Warm yourself, not the room
 These use a fraction of the power:

 An electric blanket on a 1,000 Wh unit can get you through a cold night. A space heater can’t.
 Or keep the furnace running
 If you have a gas or propane furnace, it only needs electricity for the blower, the ignition and the controls, usually 300–800 W. A power station of 2,000 Wh or more, or a generator, can often keep it going for hours and heat the whole house on gas. It does need a safe connection, normally a transfer switch or a cord-and-plug conversion for the furnace done by a licensed electrician. Our generator sizing guide covers other options.
 Low-power ways to stay warm
 Pick one room, ideally small, on an inside wall and on the sunny side, and close it off.
 Cover the windows with blankets or heavy curtains at night, and open them on sunny days.
 Block drafts under doors with towels.
 Layer up: thermal base layers, hats and wool socks.
 Use sleeping bags rated for low temperatures.
 Eat and drink something warm. A camp stove (used outside) or a thermos of hot water helps.
 Pipes
 If the house is going to drop below freezing for a while, protect the plumbing: let the faucets drip, open the cabinet doors under sinks, and know where the main water shutoff is.
 One night, planned two ways
 Take a 2,000 Wh power station, which gives you about 1,700 Wh after losses, and a cold 10-hour night.
 Plan A: the space heater. On low, at 750 W, it’s flat in about 2.3 hours, with nothing left for anything else.
 Plan B: heat the people.

 That adds up to 1,400 Wh, so you wake up warm with the food safe and about 300 Wh still in the battery. Same battery, very different night.
 Cold weather and batteries
 Power stations don’t love the cold either. Most LiFePO4 units can’t recharge below about 32°F, and capacity drops as they get colder. Keep the unit in the room you’re using rather than a freezing garage, and bring it inside well before you need to recharge it.
 If you do run a heater, plug it straight into the power station with no extension cord or power strip, and keep it at least 3 feet from bedding and curtains.
 The takeaway
 A power station can run a space heater, but only for minutes to a couple of hours. Use the battery for electric blankets, the furnace blower and the essentials, and plan other heat sources safely. Our winter power outage guide has the full plan.

 Frequently asked questions
 What is the best way to heat a room with a power station? Use low-wattage personal heat instead of room heaters: an electric blanket (50–100 W) or heated mattress pad can run all night on a mid-size power station, while a space heater would drain it in under an hour.
 Can a power station run a gas furnace? Often yes. A gas furnace only needs electricity for its blower fan and controls, typically 300–800 W running. It must be connected properly, usually through a transfer switch or a furnace power cord installed by an electrician.
 Is a propane heater safe indoors? Only heaters specifically rated for indoor use, with an oxygen depletion sensor, used according to the manufacturer's instructions and with a working CO alarm. Never use outdoor propane heaters or grills indoors.
